papers.what_it_is: A 1995 theory paper that proves a set of all one-bit quantum gates plus the two-bit XOR gate is universal and gives upper and lower bounds on the number of such elementary gates needed for controlled-U gates, Toffoli gates and arbitrary unitaries.

assertions.value: The authors state that the set of all one-bit quantum gates (U(2)) together with the two-bit exclusive-or gate is universal, in the sense that all unitary operations on arbitrarily many bits can be expressed as compositions of these gates.
quotes: We show that a set of gates that consists of all one-bit quantum gates (U(2)) and the two-bit exclusive-or gate
is universal in the sense that all unitary operations on arbitrarily many bits n (U(2n)) can be expressed as compositions of these gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: This is the abstract's summary. The exact-simulation proof for arbitrary unitaries in Section 8 is given only in outline (the authors write 'In outline, the procedure is as follows'), so the full statement is not quoted with a complete proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that they derive upper and lower bounds on the exact number of elementary gates required for a variety of two- and three-bit quantum gates and the asymptotic number for n-bit Deutsch-Toffoli gates, and make some observations about the number required for arbitrary n-bit unitary operations.
quotes: We derive upper and lower bounds on the exact number of elementary gates required to build up a variety of two- and three-bit quantum gates
the asymptotic number required for n-bit Deutsch-Toﬀoli gates
and make some observations about the number required for arbitrary n-bit unitary operations.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the paper's own scope; the individual bounds are separate assertions.

assertions.value: The paper describes the state of a quantum computer as a state vector that is a complex linear superposition of all binary states of the bits (each bit in {0, 1}), and its evolution in time as a unitary operator, a bijective, length-preserving linear transformation.
quotes: In quantum computation, the state of the computer is described by a state vector Ψ, which is a complex linear superposition of all binary states of the bits xm ∈ {0, 1}:
The state’s evolution in the course of time t is described by a unitary operator U on
this vector space, i.e., a linear transformation which is bijective and length-preserving.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 states the paper's own model of quantum computation, on which all later results depend.

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum computer with m physical bits can perform unitary operations in a space of 2 to the power m dimensions, exponentially larger than its physical size, whereas a classical simulation of unitary evolution is bounded by the number of classical degrees of freedom.
quotes: but the dimension of the unitary operator thus attainable is bounded by the number of classical degrees of freedom
By contrast a quantum computer with m physical bits (see deﬁnition of the state above) can perform unitary operations in a space of 2m dimensions, exponentially larger than its physical size.
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement made without proof in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that Shor discovered quantum polynomial time algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithm, two important natural problems for which no polynomial-time classical algorithm was known.
quotes: culminating in Shor’s [21, 22] discovery of quantum polynomial time algorithms for two important natural problems, viz. factoring and discrete logarithm, for which no polynomial-time classical algorithm was known.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (references 21 and 22).

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum gate array formalism they use was introduced by Deutsch [24], who showed that a simple generalization of the Toffoli gate (the three-bit gate ∧2(Rx)) suffices as a universal gate for quantum computing.
quotes: was introduced by Deutsch [24], who showed that a simple generalization of the Toﬀoli gate (the three-bit gate ∧2(Rx), in the language introduced later in this paper) suﬃces as a universal gate for quantum computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Deutsch (reference 24).

assertions.value: The paper defines its quantum gate array as quantum gates interconnected without fanout or feedback by quantum wires, where each gate has as many inputs as outputs and a gate of n inputs carries a unitary operation of the group U(2n) (a generalized rotation in a Hilbert space of dimension 2n, as printed).
quotes: It consists of quantum “gates”, interconnected without fanout or feedback by quantum “wires”.
The gates have the same number of inputs as outputs, and a gate of n inputs carries a unitary operation of the group U(2n),
i.e., a generalized rotation in a Hilbert space of dimension 2n.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 states the paper's own computational model.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the group as U(2n) and the dimension as 2n; these are U of 2 to the n and dimension 2 to the n.

assertions.value: The authors state that Yao has shown [27] that acyclic quantum gate arrays can simulate quantum Turing machines.
quotes: Fortunately, Yao has shown [27] that acyclic quantum gate arrays can simulate quantum Turing machines.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Yao (reference 27).

assertions.value: The authors state that DiVincenzo [28] showed two-bit universal quantum gates are possible, that Barenco [29] showed almost any two-bit gate within a certain restricted class is universal, and that Lloyd [30] and Deutsch et al. [31] showed almost any two-bit or n-bit (n ≥ 2) gate is universal.
quotes: In particular, DiVincenzo[28] showed that two-bit universal quantum gates are also possible;
Barenco[29] extended this to show than almost any two-bit gate (within a certain restricted class) is universal,
and Lloyd[30] and Deutsch et al.[31] have shown that in fact almost any two-bit or n-bit (n ≥ 2) gate is also universal.
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work (references 28 to 31).

assertions.value: The authors state that Sleator and Weinfurter [9] exhibited a scheme for obtaining the Toffoli gate with a sequence of exactly five two-bit gates, and that the authors build on that strategy.
quotes: In the present work we in part build upon the strategy introduced by Sleator and Weinfurter[9], who exhibited a scheme for obtaining the Toﬀoli gate with a sequence of exactly ﬁve two-bit gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Sleator and Weinfurter (reference 9).

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not touch at all on the great difficulties of the physical realization of a quantum computer, naming error correction [34] and quantum coherence [35, 36].
quotes: We will not touch at all on the great diﬃculties attendant on the actual physical realization of a quantum computer — the problems of error correction[34] and quantum coherence[35, 36] are very serious ones.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 states the paper's own scope limit: no treatment of physical realization, error correction or coherence.

assertions.value: The paper defines the (m + 1)-bit operator ∧m(U), with ∧0(U) equated with U; when U is the bit-flip matrix, ∧m(U) is the Toffoli gate with m+1 input bits.
quotes: deﬁne the (m + 1)-bit (2(m+1)-dimensional) operator ∧m(U ) as
Note that ∧0(U ) is equated with U .
∧m(U) is the so-called Toﬀoli gate[4] with m+1 input bits, which maps |x1, . . . , xm, y
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 defines the notation on which every later result depends.

assertions.value: The authors cite [31, 29] that almost any single ∧1(U) gate is universal in the sense that successive application to pairs of bits in an n-bit network can approximate any unitary transformation with arbitrary accuracy.
quotes: As shown by one of us [31, 29], “almost any” single ∧1(U) gate is universal in the
sense that: by successive application of this gate to pairs of bits in an n-bit
network, any unitary transformation may be approximated with arbitrary accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (references 31 and 29).

assertions.value: The authors state that the classical analogue of their universality result, that all invertible boolean functions can be implemented with the classical two-bit gate and the one-bit negation gate, is false; only a tiny fraction of Boolean functions, those linear with respect to modulo 2 arithmetic, can be generated with these gates [39].
quotes: all invertible boolean functions can be implemented with
gates[38] — is false.
it is well known that only a tiny fraction of Boolean
(those which are linear with respect to modulo 2 arithmetic) can be generated
with these gates[39].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper presents this as a well-known classical fact and cites [38] and [39], not as its own result.

assertions.value: The authors state that Toffoli showed [4] the classical ∧m gates could not be built without work bits to store intermediate results, and that by contrast they show the quantum logic gates can always be constructed with no workspace whatsoever.
quotes: Toﬀoli showed[4] that the classical ∧m’s could not be built without the presence of some “work bits” to store intermediate results of the calculation.
that the quantum logic gates can always be constructed with the use of no workspace
assertions.certainty_reason: A summary statement in the introduction; the constructions that carry it (Lemma 7.5 and Corollary 7.6) are separate assertions. Some later constructions need an extra bit (Section 7.1), so the statement is scoped to those that use none.
assertions.reader_inference: Later, Section 7.1 says its linear constructions of ∧n−2(σx) require one extra bit, so 'no workspace whatsoever' holds for the quadratic construction of Section 7.2, not for every construction in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that to implement a family of ∧m gates exactly, the time required for their implementation can be reduced from order m squared to order m merely by the introduction of one bit for workspace.
quotes: — we ﬁnd that to implement a family of ∧m gates exactly, the time required for our implementation can be reduced from Θ(m2) to Θ(m) merely by the introduction of
one bit for workspace.
assertions.certainty_reason: An introductory summary of results shown in Sections 7.1 and 7.2; the detailed results are separate assertions.

assertions.value: The paper defines a basic operation as either a ∧0(U) gate or the 2-bit reversible exclusive-or (XOR) gate, and uses the convention that time advances from left to right in the gate-array diagrams.
quotes: The third and fourth networks contain a ∧0(U) and a 2-bit reversible exclusive-or (simply called XOR henceforth) gate, respectively.
Throughout this paper, when we refer to a basic operation, we mean either a ∧0(U) gate or this 2-bit XOR gate.
In all the gate-array diagrams shown in this paper, we use the usual convention that time advances from left to right, so that the left-most gate operates ﬁrst, etc.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 defines the paper's unit of gate counting and the diagram convention.

assertions.value: The paper defines Ry(θ) as a rotation by θ around y, Rz(α) as a rotation by α around z, Ph(δ) as a phase shift with respect to δ, σx as a negation (Pauli matrix), and I as the identity matrix.
quotes: Deﬁnition: In view of the above lemma, we deﬁne the following.

assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 defines the matrices used in all later constructions.

assertions.value: Lemma 4.2 states six properties: Ry rotations add their angles under multiplication, as do Rz rotations and Ph phase shifts; σx times σx is the identity; and conjugating Ry(θ) or Rz(α) by σx negates the angle.
quotes: Lemma 4.2: The following properties hold:
Ry(θ1) · Ry(θ2) = Ry(θ1 + θ2)
σx · σx = I
σx · Ry(θ) · σx = Ry(−θ)
σx · Rz(α) · σx = Rz(−α)
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 4.2 is stated with its six properties quoted; the paper gives no separate proof, and each is a direct matrix identity.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper states Lemma 4.2 without a proof; it is a set of direct matrix identities. The quotes hold four of the six properties; the other two (Rz and Ph addition) are the same form as the first.

assertions.value: Lemma 4.3 states that for any special unitary matrix W in SU(2) there exist matrices A, B and C in SU(2) such that A · B · C = I and A · σx · B · σx · C = W; the proof gives A, B and C explicitly from the Euler-angle decomposition of Lemma 4.1.
quotes: Lemma 4.3: For any special unitary matrix W
For any special unitary matrix W (W ∈ SU(2)), there exist matrices A, B, and C ∈ SU(2) such that A · B · C = I and A · σx · B · σx · C = W
Proof: By Lemma 4.1, there exist α, θ, and β such that W = Rz(α) · Ry(θ) · Rz(β).
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 4.3 is proved on page 10 by explicit construction; its statement and condition (W in SU(2)) are quoted.
